unit.title: A Money value object as a record

fund-csharp/05-classes-properties-and-re.instructions:
**Skills:** records · value objects  
**Level:** ★★☆

**Interview prompt.** "Prices are passed around as bare decimals, and someone added euros to dollars. Introduce a Money type."

**Why it matters.** A value object bundles a value with its unit and its rules. A record gives you value equality and immutability for free; you add the domain behaviour.

**Your task.** Complete `record Money(long Cents, string Currency)` in the types section:
- `Money Add(Money other)` returns the sum as a NEW Money; adding a different currency throws `InvalidOperationException`
- `Money Times(int factor)` returns a NEW Money with the cents multiplied
- `ToString()` returns the amount with exactly two decimals, a space and the currency, using a dot as the decimal separator on every machine: 1234 cents of EUR is `"12.34 EUR"`, and -5 cents is `"-0.05 EUR"`

Equality must stay value-based: two Money values with the same cents and currency are `==`.

**Worked example.** `new Money(1250, "EUR").Add(new Money(250, "EUR"))` equals `new Money(1500, "EUR")` and prints `"15.00 EUR"`.
hints: A record already gives you value equality; you only need the arithmetic rules and the text format.

Make every operation return a modified copy instead of changing the current value, refuse to combine two different currencies, and format the amount with a fixed culture so the decimal separator never depends on the server.
Refuse to combine different currencies, build every result as a modified copy of the current value, and print the cents as a decimal amount with two places and a dot whatever the server culture is.
